At 4K, lossless is where the shape idea runs out.

The earlier rounds ran on a 512×288 crop, where the region coder appeared to edge WebP below 29.2 dB — a result that did not survive taking WebP off its default encoder setting. This is the same picture at 3840×2160, its native size, priced by the same coder. Every panel below is a 1:1 window — one screen pixel is one image pixel, no resampling, and the display copies are lossless so the artefacts are each encoder's own.

Being exactly right

What each encoder costs to reproduce all 8,294,400 pixels with zero error. The shape coder is priced with this study's own crack-edge and colour coders, with no container and no header — an idealised lower bound, competing against real files.

The partition degenerates

To be exact, every run of identical pixels becomes its own region: 6,356,392 of them across 8,294,400 pixels, averaging 1.305 px. There is no geometry left to exploit.

So the walls become free

14,508,938 crack edges cost 0.4534 bits each — when almost every pixel boundary is a wall, the wall map is nearly constant and compresses to 803 KB.

And colour is the whole bill

10.81 MB of 11.60 MB. At this point the coder is a raster coder, with one predictor where WebP has fourteen, plus a colour transform, LZ77 with 2D distances, and a colour cache.

Steps 1 and 2 have no real WebP column: at 3840×2160 cwebp bottoms out at q0 = 85,102 B, so it cannot produce a file as small as the shape coder's 19,819 B at all, and the left panel there is that floor rather than a match. Those two rows are the one place on this page where the region coder reaches somewhere WebP does not — the very bottom of the rate axis, which is exactly where report 05 said the only real argument was. Everywhere WebP can reach, it is ahead, and by more as the rate rises.

The 512×288 win does not survive

The same photograph, resampled to four sizes, each encoded by both coders and read at a fixed PSNR so the same picture quality is bought at every rung. Positive means the shape coder needs more bytes than WebP for the same result.

Boundary length grows with the linear dimension and area with its square, so a 16× pixel count should only be a 4× boundary cost — the isoperimetric term that sinks the shape coder ought to weaken at 4K. It does. The deficit still grows, because WebP's own cost per pixel falls faster: at 4K it has more correlated neighbourhood to predict from, longer LZ77 matches, and more tiles to segment its entropy image over, while the shape coder gains only a slightly better area-to-perimeter ratio.

Where the bytes actually go

Whole-image PSNR at the 200 KB operating point says WebP is 0.94 dB ahead. Measured on 448×448 windows instead, it says something more specific.

windowcontentshapesWebP gap
Sunlit ridgedense texture, hard shadow terminator26.01 dB26.44 dB-0.43 dB
Snow and rockflat fields split by sharp dark edges26.82 dB27.39 dB-0.57 dB
Skysmooth gradient, film grain36.90 dB42.29 dB-5.39 dB

Texture is a near-tie

On the ridge and the snowfield the shape coder is within 0.6 dB. Sharp edges and busy detail are what a region model is for, and it holds its own.

The gradient is the loss

The sky costs it 5.39 dB. A piecewise-constant model has one way to draw a smooth ramp — stack flat bands and pay for every boundary. A DCT spends one low-frequency coefficient.

Which is fixable, and still not enough

Report 04 priced the affine variant: linear colour per region closes most of the gradient gap and costs more in coefficients than it saves. The bands are a symptom; the explicit boundary is the disease.

Source: the macOS Sierra wallpaper at 3840×2160, decoded from a q95 JPEG — so the “original” carries JPEG artefacts and film grain that a downscale would have averaged away. Both coders see the identical PNG. Shape-coder bytes are contour + colour with no container; WebP, AVIF, JPEG XL and PNG bytes are whole files. PSNR is this study's RGB definition throughout. Codec settings: cwebp -m 6, avifenc -s 6, cjxl -e 7. A third window (snow and rock) is measured and tabulated above but not embedded, to keep this page's weight down.
